title: Orak: Training & Evaluating LLM Agents on Video Games
one_liner: Orak is a multi-game benchmark that systematically evaluates and fine-tunes language models to act like intelligent game players by chaining reflection, planning, and action modules.
lead: Video game agents need to handle messy, real-time decisions: dodge attacks, gather resources, reason through strategy. Most benchmarks are toy grids or text-only. Orak is the first standardized test for language model game agents across 12 real games (Mario, StarCraft, Poker, Minecraft) with modular reasoning strategies and a dataset of expert gameplay to teach general models how to play well.

problem.h2: Why existing game benchmarks miss the real problem
paras: Video games are messy. A language model must watch the game state (position of enemies, your health, money left), remember what happened last turn, decide what move makes sense, and execute it—all while time is running out. Existing benchmarks are either toy simulators (fake 2D grids) or measure only raw game score without studying HOW agents reason.

A beginner solution: give a language model raw game images or text descriptions and ask it to win. That fails because the model has no structure for reasoning. It guesses randomly, tries the same failed move twice, forgets key information, and never learns from mistakes. The model needs scaffolding—coached reasoning patterns that break the decision into steps: remember what worked before, plan the next subtask, then execute.

callout.html: Game benchmarks lack genre diversity, structured reasoning studies, and datasets that teach language models to play well.

panels.title: 1. The setup
panels.caption: Language model faces a game: enemies, timer, health bar, goal. What should it do?

panels.title: 2. The naive move fails
panels.caption: Model guesses randomly. Repeats failed moves. No memory, no plan, loses.

panels.title: 3. Orak's move: structured reasoning
panels.caption: At each step: reflect on what failed, plan the next subtask, then execute action.

panels.title: 4. Trained on expert gameplay
panels.caption: Benchmark provides 300+ trajectories per module showing expert reflect-plan-act sequences.

panels.title: 5. The payoff
panels.caption: Fine-tuned model recalls mistakes, adapts strategy, wins harder games consistently.

steps.text: Orak covers 12 real games across 6 genres (action, adventure, RPG, simulation, strategy, puzzle), not toy grids.
Each game plugs into a standard interface. Agentic modules (reflection, planning, action) are callable tools the LLM chains together.
At each turn: LLM reads game state, calls reflection module to critique last action, calls planning to set next subtask, then executes.
Record expert gameplay showing successful reflect-plan-act sequences across all 12 games and agentic modules.
Train general LLMs on this dataset to learn when to reflect, plan, and act—turning pretrained models into game agents.

paras: Orak does not change the language model itself. It changes what the model sees and how it decides: instead of raw game images, the model receives structured game state; instead of one giant decision, it chains three focused reasoning steps—reflection on what just happened, planning what comes next, then action execution. This turns an unstructured guess into a disciplined sequence.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: agentic module effectiveness
hidden.name: per-module performance contribution
paras: Orak measures something invisible: how much does reflection actually help? Reflection helps because when the model compares what it tried to what the game outcome was, it learns not to repeat the same move twice. Does planning matter more in strategy games than action games? Each agentic module (reflection, planning, action) contributes differently depending on the game genre and model size. This contribution is the paper's core hidden quantity—it cannot be seen in raw game score alone, but Orak's modular evaluation isolates it by running with each module enabled or disabled.

The paper estimates this by running each model configuration with and without each module, comparing scores to see which modules lift performance the most. A small model like Llama-3.2-1B may not benefit from planning (gets confused by too many steps), while a larger one needs it to handle complex strategy.

heat.caption: Darker means higher boost to game score. Shows which agentic modules help most for which games.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is the strength of each reasoning module. Reflection helps you learn from mistakes because comparing what you tried to what happened teaches you to avoid failed moves. Planning prevents random moves by forcing you to pick one concrete subtask instead of guessing. Action execution matters least if the earlier two steps are wrong, because a bad plan executed well still fails.

Orak isolates module contribution via ablation (running the pipeline with/without each module) across game genres and model sizes, revealing that reflection and planning carry most of the gain for complex games, while smaller models may not benefit from all three.

mechanism.h2: Why structured reasoning chains beat raw guesses
paras: Here is the mechanism: a language model at each game step has incomplete information (it cannot see the future) and must act fast. If it guesses randomly, it wastes actions and forgets what failed. The reflect-plan-act pipeline forces the model to slow down and think step by step: first, look at what just happened and why it failed; second, pick one concrete subtask to try next; third, commit to an action that serves that subtask. This structure prevents the model from thrashing—repeating the same failed move—because reflection forces it to notice failure.

Orak provides expert gameplay examples showing exactly when and how experts use each module. When a model is trained on these trajectories, it internalizes the pattern: if the last action failed (detected by state change), call reflection before planning the next move. For complex games like StarCraft, this discipline is critical. For simpler games, the model may ignore planning and act fast. The fine-tuning dataset teaches each model size and genre what balance works.

stages.s: Game state: positions, health, time left
Call reflection module: analyze why last action succeeded or failed
Call planning module: decide one concrete subtask to do next
Call action module: pick the move that serves that subtask
Execute action; observe new state; loop

math.words: total score equals base game score plus module contribution bonus minus penalty for wasted moves
symbols: total performance in this game run
raw points from the game (win=100, progression=50, etc.)
performance boost from agentic module i (reflection, planning, or action)
moves that did not advance the subtask

worked.title: A tiny worked example on Mario
lines: Pretrained Llama-3B, no fine-tuning: GameScore = 30 (made it to level 2), no modules, wasted 20 random jumps = 30 + 0 - 1.0*20 = 10.

Same Llama-3B, fine-tuned on Orak data: calls reflection (saved 8 wasted moves), calls planning (focused on jumping pattern), GameScore = 65 (reached level 5) = 65 + (reflection=+12, planning=+8) - 1.0*4 = 89.
Fine-tuning taught the model to reflect and plan. Without those modules it thrashes; with them it plays deliberately. The gain is not magic—it comes from practicing expert sequences.

math.note: The formula shows why structure helps: agentic modules add positive contributions (because they force deliberate reasoning instead of random guessing), while unguided moves subtract value through wasted actions (because time and game resources are finite).

bars.h2: Naive vs. structured reasoning: the numbers

charts.title: Pretrained LLM without fine-tuning
charts.note: The model guesses randomly. No scaffolding. Fails across all genres.

charts.title: Fine-tuned on Orak data
charts.note: Fine-tuning on reflect-plan-act trajectories teaches the model structured reasoning. Performance lifts across all genres. Largest gain on strategy games (planning matters most).

items.html: If the model keeps reflecting without acting, it runs out of time. Orak fine-tuning must balance reflection with decisive action.

items.b: Planning does not match action execution.
items.html: The model plans a subtask but then executes a move that does not serve it. Expert trajectories in Orak show this failure explicitly so fine-tuning learns coherence.

items.b: Genre mismatch: strategy methods applied to action games.
items.html: Careful planning is essential for StarCraft but wastes time in fast action games because you must react in milliseconds. Orak covers both genres, so the model learns which reasoning strategy fits which game by seeing expert trajectories that show when to plan deeply and when to act fast.

items.b: Done right: structured reasoning with adaptive depth.
items.html: Orak data is collected such that reflection and planning intensity match game demands. The model learns to shallow-think on action and deep-think on strategy.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a small model (Llama-3.2-1B) on raw game score from zero-shot play. Record the loss curve. It will be noisy and flat. Then fine-tune the same model on Orak trajectories for one epoch and re-run the same games. Measure win rate and average game score per genre. Plot the gains side by side: zero-shot vs. Orak fine-tuned. The demo must show that fine-tuning on structured reasoning examples (not raw game replays, but expert reflect-plan-act chains) lifts performance across action, strategy, and RPG genres.
demo.closing: The irreducible proof: a model that was randomizing becomes one that plans and reflects, proven by comparing game performance before and after learning from expert trajectories.
